column2: The ferry to the island ran twice a day in winter, once at seven in the morning and once just before dusk. Most passengers were nurses, plumbers and schoolteachers who knew the crew by name. When the swell was too heavy the captain posted a handwritten note on the ticket office door, and everyone went back up the hill to the cafe to wait. Nobody complained much; the note was usually right, and the coffee was hot.

Our village library keeps its oldest maps in a flat wooden cabinet near the radiator, which the archivist says is exactly the wrong place for paper. Every autumn she asks the council for money to move the cabinet, and every autumn the council promises to think about it. Meanwhile she wraps each sheet in acid free tissue and checks the humidity gauge with a small torch before locking up at night.

Learning to bake sourdough took me most of a year. The first loaves were dense enough to prop open a door, and the starter smelled of nail varnish for weeks. A neighbour finally explained that my kitchen was simply too cold, so I began keeping the jar on top of the fridge. Within a fortnight the dough rose properly, the crust crackled as it cooled, and I stopped buying bread from the shop.

The cycling club meets outside the post office at eight on Sunday mornings regardless of weather. Routes are chosen by whoever arrives first, which has produced some memorable detours through farm tracks and one regrettable ford. Riders carry a spare tube, a pump and something sweet to share at the halfway stop. Newcomers are told to stay near the back until they learn which riders signal potholes and which do not.

During the storm the power failed across the whole valley for almost two days. We cooked soup on a camping stove in the garage and read aloud by lantern light, taking turns with a battered adventure novel nobody had opened in years. The freezer was the real worry, so we packed it with blankets and did not open the lid once. When the lights returned at last, the children seemed almost disappointed.

My grandfather repaired clocks in a narrow workshop behind the hardware store. He worked under a green lamp with a loupe screwed into one eye, humming tunes from films he had watched as a boy. Customers left their clocks with a paper tag tied to the key, and he wrote every repair into a thick ledger in pencil. After he retired the ledger came to me, and I still find his notes surprisingly funny.

Planting the orchard meant digging forty holes in heavy clay during the wettest March anyone could remember. We lined each hole with compost from the stable, set the young apple and pear trees against stakes, and wrapped the trunks in mesh against rabbits. Three trees died that summer and were replaced the next winter. Now, eight years later, the orchard gives more fruit than the family can possibly eat, so we press the rest into juice.

The night shift at the sorting depot begins with a short briefing about which routes are short of drivers. Parcels arrive on long conveyor belts and are scanned, weighed and pushed into cages labelled by postcode. Around three in the morning the canteen opens for tea and toast, and the noise of the hall drops for twenty minutes. By six the vans are loaded, the cages are empty, and the day staff start drifting in from the car park.
